judge_assessment.explanation: I re-derived every one of the 19 checks and each matches the key and the worksheet: P(blue) = 8/20 = 2/5; sample mean 180/8 = 22.5 with mode 20; 6/40 = 3/20 and 12 x 40/6 = 80 fish; the spinner's five sections are two red, two green and one blue, so P(not red) = 3/5 and P(green) = 2/5; median 2 and total 24 pets over the twelve households; 14/50 = 7/25 and 900 x 14/50 = 252 walkers; 1/6 and 300/6 = 50 fours; median 18 with Q1 15, Q3 27 and IQR 12 for the April temperatures; 45/60 = 3/4 and 800 x 3/4 = 600. The judge's two specific claims hold: the skate-park survey is correctly identified as biased and problem 10's simulation design is acceptable, and BOTH open items — 9(c) and 10 — carry {"type": "manual"} entries, which is why manual_items_reviewed 2 is right. I also checked the two things the judge did not mention and that fail elsewhere in this batch: the Quick Answers bank renders every value (no em dash except problem 10's genuine manual-only entry, no sympify artefact), and the study guide's try-its (5/12, 300 x 7/20 = 105, median 8 with IQR 8) are all correct. I found no defect to report.

strengths_to_preserve: Problem 8 turns a classmate's wrong answer into a machine-checked object: 19 is declared as a trap with expr "31 - 12" derived from the sample's own extremes, so verify.py proved it is the range and not the IQR, and the key then names it ("the spread from the coldest day to the warmest") and explains why the range moves under one unusual day while the IQR does not.

Every open item is declared: 9(c) (why a skate-park sample cannot be trusted and what would fix it) and 10 (design a four-outcome simulation) both carry manual entries whose desc lists the components a full-credit answer must contain — random device, which outcomes stand for the event, what one trial is, how many trials, and how the results estimate the probability.

The population estimates are encoded as expressions over the stated givens rather than as typed results (t*n/m at 12/40/6 for the pond, n*f/s at 900/14/50 and 800/45/60 for the two school surveys), so the scale-up METHOD is what got verified, not just the number.

The directions block states the probability model as a formula, requires lowest terms, and says explicitly that every data set comes from a stated sample and every count and unit is given — which is exactly the "state units and givens explicitly" instruction the prompt carried.
case_summary: A clean representations-and-applications set on random samples and simple probability models. Ten realistic, uncluttered contexts — raffle drum, tagged fish, spinner, pet survey, walkers, number cube, April temperatures, skate-park bias, cereal-card simulation — with no irrelevant story detail and every count and unit stated. All 19 machine checks reproduce exactly, the scale-ups are verified as expressions over the givens rather than as typed answers, problem 8's planted 19 is a trap derived from the data, and both genuinely open items are declared manual with explicit full-credit criteria. The Quick Answers bank renders every value cleanly and the study guide's three try-its all check. I looked specifically for the two dominant failures in this run — printed slots without verify entries, and open responses recorded as machine-verified — and neither is present. Nothing meaningful to fix; the sheet compiles to five pages against a three-page budget, which is airy, but the judge and I both read the pages as usable rather than defective.
